title: China factory output grows at fastest pace in 6 months: RatingDog PMI
full_text:
Investing.com -- China’s private manufacturing sector maintained its expansion in October, with the headline PMI matching economists’ expectations and factory output growing at its fastest pace since April, according to the private sector survey released on Monday.
The RatingDog China General Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) stood at 52.0 in October, slightly below September’s 52.1 but matching economists’ expectations. The reading remained above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction for an 11th consecutive month.
In contrast, China’s official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 in October from 50.1 in September, returning to contraction territory and missing forecasts for 49.9, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
The gap between the two surveys partly reflects differences in coverage - the official gauge includes more large and state-owned manufacturers, while RatingDog has greater exposure to smaller and private firms.
The official survey showed manufacturing production and new orders weakening, with their respective sub-indexes falling to 49.8 and 49.4.
The private survey, meanwhile, pointed to stronger factory output, which increased at its fastest pace since April, supported by higher new orders from both domestic and overseas markets. Total new orders rose for a 17th consecutive month, while new export orders increased for a fourth month, although the pace of export growth eased to a three-month low.
Manufacturers increased purchasing activity to meet stronger demand, with buying activity expanding at its fastest pace in eight months. Employment growth remained marginal, however, while backlogs of work increased for a ninth consecutive month.
Price pressures remained mixed. Input costs rose for a 16th straight month, although inflation eased from September, while selling prices fell for a second time in three months as intense competition encouraged firms to offer discounts.
The Chinese yuan remained near a more than four-year high against the dollar, supported by exporters converting foreign-currency earnings into yuan, while the CSI 300 and Shanghai Composite rose 0.4% and 0.7%, respectively.

title: Binance sees outflows stabilising as exchange returns online after $6.3 billion heist
full_text:
By Rae Wee
Nov 2 (Reuters) - Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion stolen from the platform last week.
The exchange moved to reassure crypto investors and said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial" after, what analysts believe, may be the world’s biggest financial robbery ever.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday. Ether hit a two-month low on Friday and also recovered a little to $2,287.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally. It said on Sunday it had $171 billion in total assets under management as of October 28.
The Binance theft adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust Binance with their money after the attack. The exchange said it had covered 95% of the assets stolen in the heist.
Stablecoin market capitalisations tend to fall when money is leaving cryptocurrencies and they have dropped since Friday. The combined capitalisation of the two largest stablecoins, USDT and USDC, has dropped by about $1.2 billion since Friday, according to Coinmarketcap.com.
Spot bitcoin ETFs shed $643 million on Friday, the largest daily outflow of October, and more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.
"I get why, for conservative institutional investors, this is unsettling," Redbord said.
"A hack at a financial institution means stolen usernames and passwords. A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital."
PHASED WITHDRAWALS
Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using its money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may take longer to source, it said.
Despite those measures, some users were weighing options to hedge risks.
Jay Koh, vice president at the Asia Web3 AI Association, said he had not withdrawn any of his holdings from Binance, as most of his funds were held in a cold wallet, which was not impacted by the hack.
"I would not necessarily withdraw everything from Binance ... However, I do think it is prudent to review exposure, diversify custody arrangements and avoid keeping more assets on any single platform than necessary."
Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in stages, prioritising user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin.
"We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand," Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.
It added, "Rest assured that market conditions are stable."
Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited after the event.
Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $5.81 billion, up from the $4.36 billion it showed earlier. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updated figures.
"This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted)," a spokesperson for Binance said of the initial DefiLlama data.
FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT
The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.
Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.
Analysts had also pointed to North Korea’s involvement. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
US President Donald Trump, however, later on Saturday said it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved.
"We don’t know if it’s North Korea — but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters in comments posted by a White House account on X.

full_text:

The euro remained under pressure after Fitch revised France's credit outlook to negative from stable on Friday, citing worsening debt dynamics. Sterling was also little changed at $1.3387 in earlier trading.
The offshore yuan's USD/CNH pair was at 6.6523, while the onshore USD/CNY pair stood at 6.6540. The onshore yuan strengthened to 6.659 per dollar on Friday, its strongest level since June 6, 2022. It has gained around 5% against the dollar this year and was heading for a fourth consecutive monthly advance, supported partly by exporters converting dollar earnings into yuan.
Dollar, euro in focus as U.S. midterms and global rate decisions loom
Investors are focused on Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress and influence decisions over government spending and federal borrowing. Democrats are widely expected to win the House of Representatives, while the Senate contest remains less certain.
A Democratic sweep could create obstacles for data-centre and AI infrastructure investment at the state level, while the next debate over raising the U.S. debt ceiling could become particularly contentious, analysts said. October employment data due Friday will also be important for expectations surrounding the Federal Reserve's next policy move.
The Fed, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan and Reserve Bank of New Zealand all left interest rates unchanged last week, joining the Bank of Thailand. The BOJ's decision followed an 8-1 vote to hold rates at 1.25%, while the RBNZ's unexpected decision to keep its rate at 2.75% sent the New Zealand dollar down 1.2% last week.
The AUD/USD pair slipped 0.1% to $0.7024 ahead of Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia decision. The RBA is widely expected to raise its cash rate to 4.85%, a near two-decade high.
The NZD/USD pair fell 0.3% to $0.5614, extending pressure after last week's RBNZ surprise. The Bank of England and central banks in Norway and Sweden will also announce policy decisions this week. In Asia, Bank Negara Malaysia is expected to keep its rate unchanged at 2.75% on Thursday.
Won weakens as foreign flows and market volatility remain in focus
The USD/KRW pair rose 0.7% to 1,342.83, marking a relatively sharp decline for the South Korean won. The move comes against a backdrop of volatile foreign investment flows and uncertainty over the sustainability of the country's equity rally, which has been heavily driven by semiconductor and AI-related stocks.
Meanwhile, the People's Bank of China set Friday's midpoint at 6.7138 per dollar, its strongest fixing since February 2023, although it was substantially weaker than market estimates.
Monday's RatingDog private-sector survey pointed to continued expansion among manufacturers and stronger factory output, offering some support for the yuan after the contraction in the official manufacturing PMI.
Inflation releases from Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines will provide further signals on regional price pressures. DBS expects South Korean exports to accelerate year-on-year in October, with the trade surplus forecast at $43 billion. It sees Indonesia's third-quarter growth easing to 5.2% from 5.3%.
Elsewhere, the USD/IDR pair gained 0.4% to 18,171, while the USD/SGD pair advanced 0.2% to 1.2795 and the USD/MYR pair climbed 0.3% to 4.0665.

title: HSBC to open Hong Kong AI Institute following Singapore launch
full_text:
By Selena Li and Yantoultra Ngui
HONG KONG, Nov 2 (Reuters) - HSBC is setting up an artificial intelligence and emerging technology institute in Hong Kong, as the city’s largest bank steps up its AI push following a similar launch in Singapore earlier this year.
The bank aims to launch the institute in the first quarter of 2027, Chief Executive Georges Elhedery said at Hong Kong’s Fintech Week event on Monday.
The AI unit will work with Hong Kong University of Science and Technology as its anchor academic partner, Elhedery said, though he did not disclose headcount details.
He added the bank would move the centre to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis — a mega project bordering mainland China — as soon as its site there was ready.
The Hong Kong plan follows the Asia-focused lender’s announcement in July that it would hire more than 100 artificial intelligence specialists at an AI centre in rival financial hub Singapore.
The investment in AI transformation comes as banks globally cut staff due to AI-driven overhauls, with lenders such as Citi, Standard Chartered, and Barclays unveiling plans this year to cut thousands of jobs.
Around 80% of all banks in Hong Kong are already adopting AI or generative AI, Eddie Yue, chief executive of Hong Kong’s de facto central bank, told the conference.
HSBC’s Elhedery added that HSBC — one of Hong Kong’s largest private-sector employers with 28,000 local staff — was rolling out AI training for its entire global workforce of roughly 200,000 people.
"AI is going to be disruptive. It’s going to transform jobs," Elhedery said.
Separately, Yue told reporters on the sidelines of the event that the regulator would launch Project SAGE to support the use of AI agents in finance while setting guardrails to manage risks.
The HKMA will create a cross-sector expert panel to test AI agent applications and interoperability, Yue said.
He added that the HKMA would also seek views on governance, accountability, a central register of trusted agents and a possible "know your agent" standard.
"Innovation and risk management must go hand in hand," Yue said. The HKMA will expand trials of tokenised Exchange Fund Bills and examine whether regulated stablecoins can serve as a payment method, he added.

title: Top takeaways from Bernstein’s annual Global Sportswear survey
full_text:
Investing.com -- Sportswear spending is expected to rise in 2027, particularly in China and the U.S.. Still, demand for premium products is increasingly concentrated among younger and wealthier consumers, Bernstein’s annual global survey showed.
Bernstein surveyed 3,200 sportswear buyers across the U.S., China, the UK and Germany, examining spending plans, exercise habits and brand preferences in the $420 billion industry.
China led expectations for higher spending next year, with 56% of respondents planning to spend more, followed by 49% in the U.S., 40% in the UK and 28% in Germany.
Only 10% of Chinese respondents expected to spend less, compared with 23% in the U.S., 22% in the UK and 25% in Germany.
More frequent exercise was the leading reason for planned spending increases. Consumers expecting to cut purchases most often cited already owning enough sportswear or seeking cheaper products.
Bernstein found that younger shoppers and higher-income groups continued to exercise more frequently, contrasting with slowing activity among consumers aged 45 and older.
Sneaker ownership also increased across most markets as athletic footwear gained acceptance at work, school and dressier occasions. U.S. sneaker-wearing frequency was broadly flat amid interest in more formal styles.
Willingness to pay premium prices strengthened most in the U.S., particularly among affluent consumers, but softened at the highest price points in Europe and China.
Nike retained the strongest overall brand perceptions, ranking first in the U.S. for performance, quality, fashion and value, although its standing weakened in China.
Adidas remained particularly strong in Germany, and Lululemon improved in fashion rankings and across categories in China.
Among challengers, On gained ground in Germany and China, Hoka improved in quality and performance across Western markets, and Alo posted its strongest gains in the UK. Vuori’s ratings weakened in the U.S. and Germany.
Bernstein rates Nike, Adidas, and On Outperform, and Lululemon and Deckers Market-Perform.

title: US midterm campaign enters final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up
full_text:
By Andrew Goudsward, David Morgan and Nathan Frandino
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats’ hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday’s vote.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether Trump’s Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
“I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court’s next on this one,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday’s election.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
ALASKA PROBE INTENSIFIES
The Justice Department’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article, saying there had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had driven a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case.
Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot.
"I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It’s very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place on Saturday.
But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially."
MICHIGAN RIFT
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed’s feud with the rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed’s campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group’s ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize for past rhetoric about Israel.
“It’s certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day,” said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
TRUMP’S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN ON STATES
The administration, beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges could be noncitizens, has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal maneuvers have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how elections are run.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, on Saturday warned the state’s top federal judges that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request. Newsom said in a letter to the judges that the only reason to seize ballots “would be to interfere” in the count.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at “creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos,” in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska’s lieutenant governor “to do something that they’re not supposed to do.”
Even so, 76% of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from September 30 to October 5, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

title: China’s shift to new policy rate signals easier funding conditions
full_text:
SHANGHAI, Nov 2 (Reuters) - China’s central bank injected cash into the banking system on Monday, as it formally shifted its main policy rate to an overnight lending rate, a move analysts said would ease funding conditions and support the economy.
The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) injected 541 billion yuan ($81.3 billion) through overnight reverse repurchase agreements at 1.25%, according to a statement.
The central bank said last Friday that it would start to conduct overnight reverse repos every day and switch the seven-day operations to multiple rates from a single fixed one.
"The policy rate has officially shifted its anchor to the overnight rate, with the 1.25% pricing confirming the existing benchmark for funding costs," said Ming Ming, chief economist at CITIC Securities.
Analysts said the change effectively lowers the floor of China’s interest-rate framework by 15 basis points, reducing borrowing costs for financial institutions.
Although the move was not a conventional policy rate cut, it would help lower yields across the bond curve, they added.
"Judging by the initial 1.25% rate, the monetary policy stance is steering short-term interest rates downward," said Marco Sun, chief financial market analyst at MUFG (China).
The shift comes as credit concerns from state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group have unsettled the bond market and added pressure on policymakers to shore up investor confidence.
Zhaopeng Xing, senior China strategist at ANZ, said the move was equivalent to a targeted 15-basis-point rate cut for financial institutions.
"It’s effectively a red packet for financial institutions, boosting their net interest margins by about 5 basis points," Xing said.
"The aim is to stabilise profitability in the financial sector and strengthen its capacity to absorb risks," he added, noting the measure is unlikely to have a material impact on the stock market.
Separately, Chinese regulators, including the central bank, will hold meetings with financial institutions on Monday to discuss tools to support capital markets, media reported, as turbulence in stocks and bonds fuels calls for policy support.
Still, some analysts said they expect monetary stimulus to be delivered next year.
The transition was "a mark-to-market adjustment rather than a de facto rate cut, and (we) do not expect an LPR cut to follow in November," Citi analysts said in a note.
"We continue to see 2027 as the more likely window for rate cuts, while renewed credit concerns arising from Zhuhai Huafa reinforce the case for continued local debt-resolution efforts and should keep liquidity conditions loose in the interim."
The PBOC said last month that it was considering making the overnight reverse repurchase rate its main policy rate, in an effort to improve the transmission of monetary policy and support economic growth.
($1 = 6.6538 Chinese yuan)

The U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for Tuesday, are another major focus for investors, with the results expected to influence the legislative direction of President Donald Trump’s second term.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for election. Trump and Republicans are heading into the vote against a challenging backdrop, with voter discontent over high gasoline prices and the prolonged war with Iran weighing on the political climate.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll put Trump’s approval rating at 31%, its lowest level in the survey. A Democratic majority in both chambers of Congress could make it more difficult for the administration to advance its policy agenda. A divided Congress, meanwhile, could push the White House to rely more heavily on executive measures.
The election outcome could affect the outlook for fiscal policy, regulation, trade and other areas important to businesses and financial markets. title: Goldman hikes oil prices forecast on high supply disruption risks
full_text:
Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs raised its crude oil price forecasts, saying substantial downside risks to Middle East supply will sustain a large near-term risk premium despite a recovery in regional output that is proceeding as expected.
Strategists led by Daan Struyven lifted their December 2026 Brent forecast to $105 a barrel from $90, and their West Texas Intermediate forecast to $94 from $81. The 2027 average forecasts rose to $88 for Brent from $80, and to $78 for WTI from $73.
A jump in the risk premium to around $27 a barrel "now explains most of October’s crude price rally," strategists said, with spot Brent futures reaching $118. Goldman estimates Brent’s fair value was little changed in September and October, in the $90s, because global inventories, its main driver, were roughly flat as adaptation rebalanced output and consumption.
The market is now assigning more weight to escalation after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterms, the strategists said. The Polymarket-implied probability that the U.S.-Iran ceasefire ends due to escalation rises from 10% before the midterms to about 50% by Nov. 15 and about 75% by year-end.
Strategists said market participants are focused on three possible U.S. or Israeli actions against Iran: strikes on underground nuclear facilities, strikes on missile sites near the Strait of Hormuz, and broader strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure. The risk of Iran and its allies hitting Gulf oil infrastructure is likely highest in the third scenario, they noted.
The $27 premium is consistent with the market pricing a 5 million barrel-a-day drop in Middle East output lasting six months, according to Goldman Sachs. Rising prices for December 2027 and December 2028 Brent futures suggest markets also see a risk of persistent weakness in regional exports.
Goldman added a 1 million barrel-a-day global supply disruption allowance for 2027, citing the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts and broader geopolitical fragmentation.
"The timing and location of disruptions" is nearly impossible to predict, the strategists wrote.
Their base case still sees prices falling below the forwards, assuming the risk premium moderates and Persian Gulf output keeps recovering.
Risks are now "more symmetric" but still tilt to the upside, they said. Brent could reach $140 and average about $130 in 2027 if Gulf output stays 3.5 million barrels a day below its 2025 average.
On the flip side, it could fall into the $60s if output rises 2.5 million barrels a day above 2025 levels and the assumed disruption doesn’t occur.

title: Binance seeks to shore up confidence after record $6.3 billion heist
full_text:
By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft
BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Friday to shore up public confidence after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.
Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company’s total user assets and public reserves.
The exchange also said on Friday afternoon US eastern time that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Monday.
Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.
Binance’s other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance’s BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696.
’LARGEST-KNOWN THEFT’
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
"This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.
The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
TRUMP WEIGHS IN
US President Donald Trump, asked on Friday whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not know but his administration is looking into it.
"It was a hack. That’s the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. "But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control."
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.
The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."
The Secret Service said that its investigators "are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating license, said it is "engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident." Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
SECURITY IMPLICATIONS
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin’s most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
"Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient," Saylor wrote on Friday.
335 MILLION REGISTERED USERS
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.
On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humor, confidence in the exchange’s financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.
The reaction stood in contrast to the panic surrounding the collapse of FTX in November 2022, when mounting doubts about the exchange’s ability to repay customer funds triggered outrage online.
"Looking at all past data, we find that hot wallet hacks — even large ones — have historically not had a meaningful impact on future crypto returns," said Matt Hougan, chief investment officer at Bitwise Asset Management. "Investors tend to treat them as ’one-off events.’"

title: German retail sales plunge 2% in September, missing forecasts

Food retail sales decreased 1.4% in real terms and 1.1% in nominal terms in September compared to August. Year-over-year, food sales declined 1.1% in real terms and 0.5% in nominal terms.

title: BoE expected to hike rates this week. More to follow? Economists weigh in
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Bank of England (BoE) is widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 basis points to 4% on Thursday, and economists at ING and Goldman Sachs both see a second increase in February.
Both firms expect a 7-2 vote. ING’s developed markets economist James Smith said the two doves, Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, "are deeply sceptical of the need for higher rates."
Goldman economists, led by James Moberly, pointed to rising energy prices, firmer activity data and recent signals from Governor Andrew Bailey and the deputy governors of openness to tightening.
Smith said the move is about risk, not current data. The bank is "hiking not because the economic data is telling it to, but because of the risks presented by sharply higher energy prices," he wrote.
The economist said there is little sign of second-round effects so far, with private-sector wage growth at 3.4%, but that 4% inflation is a line the BoE has flagged as raising that risk. ING expects headline inflation to peak slightly above 4% early next year, helped by a roughly 25% rise in the household energy price cap in January.
Goldman expects the Bank’s new forecasts to show a higher near-term inflation peak of about 4.5% in the first half of 2027, and a larger medium-term undershoot because of a higher Bank Rate path. The bank sees activity firmer than expected, tracking third-quarter growth at 0.7%, three-tenths above the BoE’s estimate, and said unemployment unexpectedly dropped in August.
Looking further ahead, Smith said "there’s little precedent for ’one-and-done’ rate rises," and noted that the Bank may avoid saying so. He expects non-committal guidance, with a hawkish surprise only if the Bank signals "some further tightening" is likely.
Goldman now expects a second hike to 4.25% in February, citing continued energy pressure and stronger activity and labor data, while expecting guidance to stop short of a strong steer.
Both think markets have gone too far. Smith noted more than four hikes are priced by this time next year, and that Chief Economist Huw Pill has indicated such pricing looks unlikely.
Goldman economists called market pricing for over 100 basis points of tightening over the next year "too high," given contained wage effects and an expected slowdown in consumer spending over the winter.
Smith also said sterling is trading well on the rate outlook, with EUR/GBP down nearly 4% in about a month and speculators still running sizable short positions in the pound.
